articles.text: As 2023 closed out and 2024 waited to take stage center, I found myself thinking about time. It’s abstract, invisible. And yet, ultimately, it’s all we have. The infinite is the finite and therefore, gradually, even painfully, we come to understand that time is of the essence. We acknowledge its presence in our lives by marking its passage, making the intangible tangible: birthdays, anniversaries, holidays. We glance at clocks, wear time on our wrists, check our cell phones, keep calendars, name the months that become years. All of the above brings me to that global celebration of a year ending and another beginning, often prompting, for many of us, a silent or shared New Year’s Resolution, one predicated on a promise. Indeed, resolution, resolve, resolute are all strong words that convey intent. But I would suggest that a NYR not be too weighted or require a monastic, disciplined effort. Best to gently frame it for the long haul. Neither guilt nor nudging disappointment should be the outcome. When I considered a resolution for 2024 the words “Be Kind” came to mind. Embedded in this resolution is the belief that kindness is underrated, especially in this moment of national acrimony, made manifest in the tone of our national discourse and sense of discontent. Place that discontent in the context of politics and it’s a dark, divisive, worrying tableau. The antidote to this national mood is to be kind at every opportunity, and be mindful that every interaction, however brief or transactional, can be defined or reframed by kindness. Once again, time is, indeed, of the essence. Best wishes for 2024. articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California’s highly anticipated White Elephant Sale will return this year with 16 days of public shopping from January 31 through February 24 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. The annual preview sale, on Sunday, January 28, is sold out. New merchandise is added throughout the sale culminating in the final blow-out sale on Saturday and Sunday, March 2-3, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Known as Northern California’s biggest rummage sale, the White Elephant Sale is run exclusively by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board, a group of more than 100 year-round members, who raise money to support the museum’s art acquisitions, exhibitions, educational programs, and capital improvements. Since the Board’s inception in 1959, it has contributed over $23 million to the Museum. The Sale also boasts many volunteers from Piedmont, most of whom are members of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. To purchase tickets ($5 per day for public shopping days; tickets required for blow out sale) and learn how to donate items to the sale, visit whiteelephantsale.org. Scan to book your estimate!

articles.text: Construction begins at intersection of Nova & Magnolia Ave. The traffic island at the intersection of Nova Ave. & Magnolia Ave., dubbed “Bollard Island” by community members, may not have its signature nickname for much longer. The Public Works Department recently began a construction project that will replace Bollard Island with a raised concrete-curbed median traffic island, thus eliminating the need for its plastic bollards. Additionally, a single bulb-out will be added at the corner of the island closest to 101 Magnolia Ave as part of a “traffic calming” measure. “The goal of the bulb out is to narrow roadways,” explained Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “We’re trying to give pedestrians less distance to cross and give vehicles a lesser area to navigate. When vehicles are given more space, the faster they’re able to go.” Gonzales said that the new island, when finished, will be a greater safety aid to the community than the use of bollards. “The original bollards were not placed in a way that made them an effective traffic calming measure. This project is meant to rectify that.” For more information on construction projects in your area, please contact the Public Works Department at 420-3050 or email Director Daniel Gonzales at dgonzales@piedmont.ca.gov. Staff photo Soon, Bollard Island will lose its signature plastic bollards in favor of a raised, concrete-curbed meridian.
articles.title: “Bollard Island” to lose its bollards

articles.text: Piedmont resident Chris Moore to run on a platform of public safety Piedmont resident and local activist Chris Moore has decided to run for 5th District County Supervisor on a platform that highlights public safety as his campaign’s number one concern. Following the unexpected retirement of longtime Supervisor Keith Carson, Moore is one of nine candidates running for the 5th District seat, which includes Albany, Piedmont, Emeryville, Berkeley, and sections of north and west Oakland. Moore has been a resident of Piedmont for 22 years and is a former member of the City of Piedmont’s budget committee. Readers may also recognize Moore from his activities with Piedmont Neighbors Together, a local activist group that promotes public safety reform and crime prevention. The group gained the attention of the community in September 2023 during a surprise demonstration outside Piedmont City Hall ahead of Police Chief Jeremy Bowers’ quarterly crime report. The group advocated for change in Piedmont’s crime prevention strategies, emphasizing a need for greater police deterrence. Since then, Moore has continued to be active in local politics. Moore kicked off his campaign at a launch party on Saturday, January 13, at Le Cheval in Oakland. The location is no doubt symbolic, as Le Cheval was one of several businesses in Oakland that closed in 2023 citing rising crime. “Over 6,000 businesses chose not to renew their business licenses in Oakland last year, and that is because of the crime problem. So, yes, I want to support public safety and stop this excessive and violent crime aimed at our local businesses,” said Moore. If elected, Moore said he will use his position as County Supervisor to further public safety in the 5th District by allocating funding away from organizations without “actionable results” on public safety and placing them with organizations that have more of an effect on preventing crime. “I’m not doing this for the politics. I’m doing this for the people of Alameda County. I truly am,” he said. Moore is one of two Piedmont residents running for this position. Lorrel Plimier, president of the Piedmont League of Women Voters, is also running for a seat on the County Board of Supervisors. For more information on Chris Moore’s campaign, voters can visit www.chrismooreforsupervisor.com. Election Day will be on March 5, 2024. For more information on your local poll station, visit the California Secretary of State’s website at www.sos.ca.gov/elections/polling-place. Photo by Thomas Hawk Chris Moore talks with a supporter on Saturday, January 13, at the launch of his campaign as a candidate for a seat on the Alameda County Board of Supervisors.
articles.title: Local activist runs for county supervisor

articles.text: At its meeting on Wednesday, January 10, Piedmont School Board members were advised by middle school, high school and Millennium HS counselors on what kind of counseling most helps their students. Prefacing the counselors’ presentation, PHS English teacher and Association of Piedmont Teachers union president Dr. Elise Marks said, “We all know that our students are extremely high achieving, but that doesn’t mean they aren’t also high-needs. Our kids push themselves hard and need support.” Compared to nearby districts like Oakland and Berkeley, which “may have only one counselor for every 300 or 400 students,” PHS is at about the maximum ratio recommended by the American School Counseling Association of one counselor for 250 students. “Because we lost a PMS counselor at the start of this year, their caseload is now [1 per 415 students].” This caseload entails “organized chaos,” said Piedmont Middle School counselor Amy Sharp. “It’s a juggling act to make a daily plan prioritizing middle school students’ needs with everyone’s schedules,” she said. Collaboration has been a key to direct student support, she added. Large groups are especially helpful for academic counseling like grade-level skills, attendance and orientations, while common student needs like tech use and [its mental health effects] often involve large meetings with parents, administration and the wellness center. At the high school level, mental health support is more deeply intertwined with other areas of counseling like academic management, personal lives and future plans, said PHS counselor Amanda Carlson. PHS counselors collaborate frequently with the College and Career Center, and much one-on-one talk involves juggling graduation requirements with personal time management and lifestyle health, while also encouraging interests that students may not know they could pursue as careers. articles.text: Though Piedmont students and parents are already halfway through the school year, a new calendar year brings with it new state laws. Here are some of the most important measures passed by the California legislature taking effect in January 2024. Media literacy in every grade Per AB 873, California’s K-12 public school students will be required to learn from media literacy instruction which will help them identify fake news posted online while also being able to tell the difference between legitimate news articles and paid advertising. Critical engagement with online media content will be incorporated into the four core curricula of English language arts, mathematics, science and history / social science. Prohibited suspension for willful defiance SB 274 extends an existing prohibition against suspending students for willful defiance in grades 6 through 12, effective through July 1, 2029. “Willful defiance” includes students disrupting school activities or defying the authority of a teacher or administrator. Licensed school nurses AB 1722 allows school districts to hire licensed vocational nurses to be supervised by a credentialed school nurse if a credentialed nurse is not available to fill the licensed nurse’s job. Excused religious and personal absences Under existing law, students cannot be excused from school for more than four hours per semester to attend a religious retreat. AB 1503 expands this provision, allowing students to be excused for a full day. Although religious retreats are the only “justifiable personal reason” specified in the digest of this bill, others include “an appearance in court,” “attendance at a funeral service” and “attendance at an employment conference.” Expanded punishment for hate crimes AB 2282 increases the consequences for anyone who “places or displays hate symbols on private and nonprivate property, with the intent to terrorize another.” These symbols include Nazi swastikas, nooses, and desecrated crosses or other religious symbols. Although the increased prison sentence and maximum fines apply to hate crimes in general, the bill also expands the places where hate symbols are banned, to include K-12 schools, colleges, universities and public spaces. Involuntary leave salary AB 472 requires a classified school district or community college employee “placed on an involuntary leave of absence while the employee has criminal charges, a criminal investigation, or an administrative matter pending,” to be fully compensated for the leave period if the investigation concludes in the employee’s favor. Opioid overdose prevention SB 10 requires any school serving grades 7 through 12 to establish safety plans including protocols for responding to an opioid overdose. The bill encourages “county offices of education to establish a County Working Group on Fentanyl Education in Schools, as provided, for the purposes of outreach, building awareness, and collaborating with local health agencies regarding fentanyl overdoses.” Adequate school meals SB 348 requires “each school district, county superintendent of schools, and charter school to make available a nutritionally adequate breakfast and … lunch, free of charge during each school day, to any pupil who requests a meal, without consideration of the pupil’s eligibility for a federally funded free or reduced-price meal.” It also requires schools to “provide pupils with adequate time to eat, as determined by that school district, county superintendent of schools, or charter school.” Firing a superintendent or assistant superintendent Per SB 494, school districts can’t fire a superintendent or assistant superintendent at a special or emergency school board meeting, or within 30 days after the board’s first meeting after an election. To fire without cause, the board would have to hold a regular public meeting with a 72-hour notice.
articles.title: New school laws to take effect this month

articles.text: Piedmont Play School welcomes all interested families to its open house this Saturday, January 20, from 10:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. at 401 Hampton Road, Piedmont. Meet the teachers, hear from current parents, and learn about this play-based cooperative preschool for children ages 3-5 years The Open House is for parents only. Those interested may RSVP to orianasyed@piedmontplayschool.org. If you’re new to the area, Piedmont Play School is located at Hampton Field in the most picturesque park setting. If you aren’t new to Piedmont, you might know that Piedmont Play School was established in 1958 by a small group of parents wanting to start a parent cooperative school. Piedmont Play School was first located at the Piedmont Community Church then moved adjacent to Wildwood Elementary, for three years below Community Hall, and currently is at the cozy cottage building at Hampton Field. It has 18 students ages 3 to 5, three teachers and one volunteer parent each day. Classes are in session from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m. Monday to Friday. Its calendar year is similar to Piedmont School District. As a cooperative, every parent takes on a job to help class run smoothly. Michelle Ritchie started teaching at the school in 2013 and became its Director three years later. She knows she has big shoes to fill after hearing about the legendary, dedicated teachers that came before her. Ritchie’s staff works every day to keep the school’s legacy thriving and to give the students a wonderful preschool experience based on their needs and interests. “I am a huge advocate of learning through play and I feel honored and privileged to serve our local community,” Ritchie said. “My co-teachers and I strive to provide a safe and nurturing environment where children can feel comfortable to express themselves and make lifelong companions.” Rewards of the co-op model are abundant – the opportunity to have more insight into your child’s day, have a tight-knit community that strives to organize extracurricular family activities and friendships that can last a lifetime. If you are interested in more information, plan on attending the Annual Open House on Saturday, January 20 from 10 am-12pm. For more information, e-mail orianasyed@piedmontplayschool.org. Director and head teacher Michelle Ritchie enjoys playing with the children at Piedmont Play School.
articles.title: Piedmont Play School open house on January 20

The bill encourages “county offices of education to establish a County Working Group on Fentanyl Education in Schools, as provided, for the purposes of outreach, building awareness, and collaborating with local health agencies regarding fentanyl overdoses.” Adequate school meals SB 348 requires “each school district, county superintendent of schools, and charter school to make available a nutritionally adequate breakfast and … lunch, free of charge during each school day, to any pupil who requests a meal, without consideration of the pupil’s eligibility for a federally funded free or reduced-price meal.” It also requires schools to “provide pupils with adequate time to eat, as determined by that school district, county superintendent of schools, or charter school.” Firing a superintendent or assistant superintendent Per SB 494, school districts can’t fire a superintendent or assistant superintendent at a special or emergency school board meeting, or within 30 days after the board’s first meeting after an election. To fire without cause, the board would have to hold a regular public meeting with a 72-hour notice.

articles.text: Piedmont High School actors will perform the dark musical Cabaret, directed and choreographed by Amy Moorhead, Thursday through Sunday, February 1 to February 4 at the Alan Harvey Theater on the school campus. Written by John Kander and Fred Ebb, the story is set in a Berlin nightclub as the 1920’s draw to a close. It explores the exhilarating and tumultuous life in Berlin as Germany slowly yields to the emerging Third Reich. (The director has chosen to eliminate the use of swastikas and military uniforms in this production.) Winner of the Tony Award for Best Musical in 1967, Cabaret continues to have an impact its audience and performers. “Performing in Cabaret has been a unique and profound experience for me as a Jewish high school student taking on the role of Herr Shultz,” explained PHS sophomore Ben Wakefield. “The Israel-Hamas War, which The Tony Award-winning musical Cabaret premieres at Piedmont High School on Thursday, February 1, and runs through February 4. unfolded during our rehearsals, did impact my feelings about performing in the show. It heightened my awareness of the persistent relevance of the themes explored in the musical.” “Being part of Cabaret has allowed me to engage with history, art, and my own identity in a profound way. It has underscored the importance of using the performing arts as a platform for exploring and understanding the complexities of the human experience, both past and present,” Wakefield added.” More than 60 high school students are involved in the show, including a student orchestra conducted by PHS Band Director Trevor Meseroll. Vocal Direction is handled by local professional Sandra Peter. The cast features Amelia Addington as Sally Bowles, Caitlin Boothby as the Emcee, Theo Ferguson as Cliff Bradshaw, Ben Wakefield as Herr Schultz, Ellie Broscow as Fräulein Schneider, Clare Weiss as Fräulein Kost, and Ford Andrews as Ernst. Performances are at 7 p.m. Tickets are $30 reserved, $25 adult general admission, $24 65+, $16 youth) and are available online at showtix4u.com/ event-details/80097 and at the box office. For more information, contact PHS theater director and choreographer Amy Moorehead at amoorhead@piedmont.k12.ca.us.
articles.title: PHS premiers musical Cabaret starting Feb. 1

articles.text: 2024 is here, and this year we’ll have the opportunity to witness a spectacular sight – a total solar eclipse. A total solar eclipse occurs when the moon travels between the Sun and Earth, fully blocking the face of the Sun. When the moon reaches this point where it fully blocks the Sun, it has reached totality. During this period of totality, the skies will darken, and the outermost portion of the Sun will become visible. This is known as the Sun’s corona, and it is usually concealed by the brightness of the Sun. Eclipses allow us to witness the Sun in a truly unique way and this year we will be having the chance to witness the last total solar eclipse visible from the contiguous United States until 2044. The Path of Totality The eclipse will take place on April 8, 2024, and its path of totality will extend through parts of Mexico, the United States, and Canada. To witness the total solar eclipse, observers will need to be within the path of totality. This year’s total solar eclipse is projected to last slightly over four minutes and the closer to the center of the path, the longer the period of totality will last. If you are viewing from outside the path of totality you may still have the chance to experiA solar eclipse will take place on April 8, 2024. ence a partial solar eclipse. A partial solar eclipse happens when the moon travels between the Sun and Earth, partially blocking the surface of the Sun. Observe Safely It is never safe to observe the sun without using proper specialized eye protection. Always remember to use special solar glasses, also known as eclipse glasses. When purchasing eclipse glasses ensure they meet international standards for filters used to view the Sun. It is also never safe to observe through unfiltered camera lenses, binoculars, or telescopes. Separate professional solar filters must always be used. Eclipses are an incredible sight to see but remember safety comes first. The Countdown Begins As we begin counting down the days, we invite you to join us at Chabot Space & Science Center where we’ll have the chance to experience this celestial event from Chabot’s Observation Deck. In Oakland, we will be in 34% totality, meaning 66% of the Sun’s face will be covered by the Moon. To learn more visit chabotspace.org. Isabel Lopez Ramirez is with Chabot Space and Science Center, located at 10000 Skyline Boulevard in the Oakland hills.
articles.title: Thinking Outside the Classroom Celestial Event of the Year: A Total Solar Eclipse

articles.text: The Havens Dads Club will host its 16th Annual Havens Poker Night this Friday, January 20 at the Veterans Hall. A beginner tutorial starts at 6:00 p.m., the first cards will be dealt at 6:30 p.m. and the night will continue until the sold-out field of competing bluffers and betters are whittled down to one champion. All proceeds from the event will support Havens Elementary School projects. Previous projects included partial funding for the Becker Field replacement, the Ellen Driscoll mural, lunch tables and awnings on campus, and playground blocks. The tournament, themed “All in the for Kids,” will feature professional card dealers and poker tables, with an unlimited re-buy-in format to allow for players on full-tilt to utilize their gambling skills. Hors-d’oeuvres, alongside an open snack bar, will be provided by Piedmont chef Robert Dorsey, and Top Dog. Adult beverages for sale will include cocktails, beer, and wine with Havens Dad mixologist Peter Day in charge. While buy-in tickets ($130) are limited to a waitlist, spectators may join in on the fun by purchasing a bottomless pint drink ticket at bit.ly/48CROMI.

articles.text: My name is Kane Crawford-Jakubiak, and I am a Life Scout in Piedmont Troop 11. I am working on my Eagle Scout Project with the Piedmont Historical Society. My project will help the Piedmont Historical Society by video recording interviews of former Piedmont Scouts and scouters from the 1930’s-1990’s who are willing to share their stories of what it was like to be a Scout or scouter in Piedmont back then. The goal of the project is to help the Piedmont Historical Society document and preserve this unique aspect of Piedmont’s history. I will be working with current Piedmont Scouts to video record the interviews. Piedmont is one of the oldest Scouting Councils in the country and Scouting has always been an important part of our community. I hope my project will be able to preserve these stories for future generations. If you are interested in telling your Scouting story, please contact me to set up a time for an interview. I can be reached at piedmontscoutinghistory@gmail.com.
articles.title: Calling all former Piedmont Scouts and Scouters

articles.text: “Roaring Twenties” theme on Feb. 10 celebrates Wildwood Elementary’s 100th anniversary The Wildwood Dads Club will host its annual Crab Feed on Saturday, February 10 in the Veterans Hall from 6 to 11 p.m., with dinner starting at 7:00 p.m. The event will celebrate the 100th anniversary of Wildwood Elementary School. Tickets for this year’s event, themed “The Roaring Twenties,” are now on sale – and going fast, said Scott Zengel, President of the Wildwood Dads Club. With the addition of drinks and dancing, the club expects over the capacity of 150 Crab Feed attendees at this year’s event, which will include fresh Dungeness crab, oven-roasted salmon, New Orleans-style spicy spinach, baked macaroni and cheese, scalloped potatoes, coffee and— back by popular demand— tuxedo chocolate mousse cake for dessert. “Given that we’re taking a page out of the history books, the whole event will be focused on the period when Wildwood Elementary was founded, and we’ve been working with the Piedmont Historical Society to put together a presentation on the history of the school to share at the feed,” Zengel said. “The Crab Feed is our biggest event of the year, and we sell out every year, so we’re excited to bring the community together to eat delicious crab, dance and give back to Piedmont.” All proceeds will benefit the Piedmont Beautification Foundation’s Sustainable Landscaping Project for the Piedmont Community Pool, Zengel added The crab feed is an adults-only event which includes bottomless beer and wine and dancing after dinner from 8:30 to 11 p.m. Specialty cocktails are available for purchase as well. Per the theme, this year’s dress code is Roaring Twenties-themed. Entertainment will be provided by DJ Ben Anderson, a Wildwood dad. For tickets ($75-$125), see wildwooddadsclub.org/crab-feed.
articles.title: Wildwood Crab Feed tickets selling fast

articles.text: Renee Taharka, 3rd grade Let us stand up Let us push through the barriers that hold us back To let go of the prejudice and stereotypes that float around us Let us be the ones that open our eyes to the people Let us be a concerned generation The ones who see the problems And the solutions Let’s be the ones who solve the wrongs that we all commit To help heal the wounds that no one will ever admit Let us remain awake through a great revolution Let us open our eyes to find a solution To see the world as other people see it Maybe then we can find resolution Let us be the ones who fix these mistakes Let us be the ones who stop the flames Let us be the generation who remains awake this feeling every day. Some people never feel this. Some people cause this. by bullying. Or by cyberbullying. But no matter what or who it is, this shouldn’t be an everyday feeling. Over the past couple years, it feels as if bullying, racism and sexism have just faded away. People are only thinking about the current violence, and wars. People have started to think, “if it’s not me then why would I care?” But when people just give up and stop helping, then think of how much worse it’s getting for people experiencing this. I do see that violence is a major issue. Many people are being robbed, and having their belongings stolen. But some people just let other issues go. For example, when a family sits down at a dinner table, no one says, “racism is a major issue, and it needs to stop.” Instead, everyone goes straight to the violence, and how annoying it is that their car window was broken last night. When people influence other people, it spreads. For example, when a parent, or trusted adult tells a young child about racism and bullying, they can learn to prevent bullying and stand up for others being bullied. If a child doesn’t learn about this, they may not recognize the fact that they are being bullied. For example, a young child goes to school. Let’s say they’re in preschool. They get bullied, or an older kid says a racist comment to them. They are unaffected and continue with their day. This is because their parents have yet to tell them what racism is and how bad it is. Now that’s just horrible. Someone saying a racist comment to an innocent child who is unaware. Another big issue is cyberbullying. Unlike bullying, you can’t really prevent cyberbullying without reporting it which takes a while. Cyberbullying can be done in different ways. One may hack or steal passcodes, while another may bully in a text, or in a game chat. You may think this is not a big deal, but when you think about it, you know that it is. One reason is because it may hurt even more when someone says a racist or rude comment online than in person. This may be because you don’t necessarily know who the person is, or because you can’t fully understand people in a text or chat. This may be a problem because when you are talking to someone in person you can understand their tone and see their facial expressions, but when you are online you don’t really know how the person is feeling. All of these issues relate, because racism is a form of bullying, and bullying can happen online (cyberbullying). All of these issues must come to a stop. The simplest way to prevent these issues would just be reporting it when it happens. When you start to get involved, it can lead to even bigger problems. I hope that you can understand these issues and learn more on how to stop them. Martin Luther King Jr. made a speech called “I’ve Been to the Mountaintop” He made this speech on April 3rd, 1968, in Memphis, Tennessee. It was one of Martin Luther King’s many speeches, it was also his last. This speech was delivered one day before he was assassinated at the Lorraine Motel on April 4th. It was about the Memphis sanitation strike. He delivered this speech in hopes that the workers of Mason Temple in Memphis would find it encouraging and supportive. He told the overflowing crowd, “But it really doesn’t matter now, because I’ve been to the mountaintop...I’ve seen the promised land.” He said this meaning, he has “been to the mountaintop” and seen the promised land, a place where black people have equal rights and peace. He called for unity, boycotts, and nonviolent protest, such as public assemblies and peaceful marches. Martin Luther King has made many inspiring speeches, like the “I have a Dream” speech on August 28, 1963. This speech was performed to end economic and employment injustice. But “I’ve Been to the Mountaintop” is another iconic speech. In this speech, he uses the words “I would” a lot to show the things he would do for the workers at Mason Temple. In this speech, he told the crowd in Memphis, “We, as a people, will get to the promised land.” Martin Luther King was a trailblazing civil rights leader, who made paths that were never even thought of before. He made a way for white and black people to have equal rights. But people still are treated unfairly because of their race, skin color, religion, gender, and more. Why can’t we listen to his words? Take a moment and think about that. Why are we still doing this? People are being treated like slaves just because of the way they look. Why can’t we realize that it’s the inside that matters? He said some amazing things that day, but one of the best things that he said was, “Let us stand up. Let us be a concerned generation. Let us remain awake through a great revolution.” To me this means that we need to stand up for what we think is right. To me it also means that we need to be a part of the change coming ahead. We need to be a part of the change coming for people of color. In conclusion, Martin Luther King Jr. was a trailblazing civil rights leader, he blazed the way for many famous people of color who were inspired by Martin Luther King Jr. Even including Barack Obama! He was an amazing role model, trailblazer, and civil rights activist who made paths for many people. He made so many amazing speeches, but the one on April 3rd was one of the most inspirational speeches he had ever made! Most of the things he said that day will never be forgotten. pages.text: Wednesday, January 17, 2024 9 Art & Essay winners from 3rd annual MLK Jr. Showcase Piedmont’s 27th annual Martin Luther King Jr. Celebration on Monday, January 15, concluded with the display of Piedmont student artwork and literature in the Alan Harvey Theater. This was the third year Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC) has hosted the student showcase, with 40 submissions from K-12 students. Recordings of student voices read aloud some of the poems projected onto the stage. Renee Taharka, 3rd grade Awake By Elsa Chun, 8th grade Let us stand up Let us push through the barriers that hold us back To let go of the prejudice and stereotypes that float around us Let us be the ones that open our eyes to the people Let us be a concerned generation The ones who see the problems And the solutions Let’s be the ones who solve the wrongs that we all commit To help heal the wounds that no one will ever admit Let us remain awake through a great revolution Let us open our eyes to find a solution To see the world as other people see it Maybe then we can find resolution Let us be the ones who fix these mistakes Let us be the ones who stop the flames Let us be the generation who remains awake The Real World By Lily Gurvitz, 5th grade Have you ever felt like you don’t belong? Like you shouldn’t be here? Some people get this feeling every day. Some people never feel this. Some people cause this. by bullying. Or by cyberbullying. But no matter what or who it is, this shouldn’t be an everyday feeling. Over the past couple years, it feels as if bullying, racism and sexism have just faded away. People are only thinking about the current violence, and wars. People have started to think, “if it’s not me then why would I care?” But when people just give up and stop helping, then think of how much worse it’s getting for people experiencing this. I do see that violence is a major issue. Many people are being robbed, and having their belongings stolen. But some people just let other issues go. For example, when a family sits down at a dinner table, no one says, “racism is a major issue, and it needs to stop.” Instead, everyone goes straight to the violence, and how annoying it is that their car window was broken last night. When people influence other people, it spreads. For example, when a parent, or trusted adult tells a young child about racism and bullying, they can learn to prevent bullying and stand up for others being bullied. If a child doesn’t learn about this, they may not recognize the fact that they are being bullied. For example, a young child goes to school. Let’s say they’re in preschool. They get bullied, or an older kid says a racist comment to them. They are unaffected and continue with their day. This is because their parents have yet to tell them what racism is and how bad it is. Now that’s just horrible. Someone saying a racist comment to an innocent child who is unaware. Another big issue is cyberbullying. Unlike bullying, you can’t really prevent cyberbullying without reporting it which takes a while. Cyberbullying can be done in different ways. One may hack or steal passcodes, while another may bully in a text, or in a game chat. You may think this is not a big deal, but when you think about it, you know that it is. One reason is because it may hurt even more when someone says a racist or rude comment online than in person. This may be because you don’t necessarily know who the person is, or because you can’t fully understand people in a text or chat. This may be a problem because when you are talking to someone in person you can understand their tone and see their facial expressions, but when you are online you don’t really know how the person is feeling. All of these issues relate, because racism is a form of bullying, and bullying can happen online (cyberbullying). All of these issues must come to a stop. The simplest way to prevent these issues would just be reporting it when it happens. When you start to get involved, it can lead to even bigger problems. I hope that you can understand these issues and learn more on how to stop them. Reflections on I’ve Been to the Mountaintops By Eloise Reilly, 5th grade Martin Luther King Jr. made a speech called “I’ve Been to the Mountaintop” He made this speech on April 3rd, 1968, in Memphis, Tennessee. It was one of Martin Luther King’s many speeches, it was also his last. This speech was delivered one day before he was assassinated at the Lorraine Motel on April 4th. It was about the Memphis sanitation strike. He delivered this speech in hopes that the workers of Mason Temple in Memphis would find it encouraging and supportive. He told the overflowing crowd, “But it really doesn’t matter now, because I’ve been to the mountaintop...I’ve seen the promised land.” He said this meaning, he has “been to the mountaintop” and seen the promised land, a place where black people have equal rights and peace. He called for unity, boycotts, and nonviolent protest, such as public assemblies and peaceful marches. Martin Luther King has made many inspiring speeches, like the “I have a Dream” speech on August 28, 1963. This speech was performed to end economic and employment injustice. But “I’ve Been to the Mountaintop” is another iconic speech. In this speech, he uses the words “I would” a lot to show the things he would do for the workers at Mason Temple. In this speech, he told the crowd in Memphis, “We, as a people, will get to the promised land.” Martin Luther King was a trailblazing civil rights leader, who made paths that were never even thought of before. He made a way for white and black people to have equal rights. But people still are treated unfairly because of their race, skin color, religion, gender, and more. Why can’t we listen to his words? Take a moment and think about that. Why are we still doing this? People are being treated like slaves just because of the way they look. Why can’t we realize that it’s the inside that matters? He said some amazing things that day, but one of the best things that he said was, “Let us stand up. Let us be a concerned generation. Let us remain awake through a great revolution.” To me this means that we need to stand up for what we think is right. To me it also means that we need to be a part of the change coming ahead. We need to be a part of the change coming for people of color. In conclusion, Martin Luther King Jr. was a trailblazing civil rights leader, he blazed the way for many famous people of color who were inspired by Martin Luther King Jr. Even including Barack Obama! He was an amazing role model, trailblazer, and civil rights activist who made paths for many people. He made so many amazing speeches, but the one on April 3rd was one of the most inspirational speeches he had ever made! Most of the things he said that day will never be forgotten. Caroline Kittredge, 3rd grade Lucia Gonzalez Fenton, 6th grade My Wish By Audrey Shim, 3rd grade I have a wish that everybody can be treated equally. And that people will notice when people need some kindness or help with something. I have a wish that the new generation will have a concern for equality and try to fix the cracks in our country and communities. I have a wish that people will notice when change happens. And see an example of freedom and kindness. So they know how to be kind to each other and to themselves. Alice Day, 3rd grade Bryn Balzan, 3rd grade

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. articles.text: Natalia Martinez dazzles with 41 points Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team appears to still be the class of the Western Alameda County Conference after defeating Bishop O’Dowd 59-50 at Binks Rawlings Gym on Wednesday, January 10. They also walloped league foe St. Joseph 72-33 on Friday, January 12 before losing a non-league game to Rancho Christian, 55-45, at an MLK Showcase at St. Mary’s of Stockton on Saturday, January 13. The victory over O’Dowd puts Piedmont on-track for its second-consecutive WACC title. “We haven’t played since December 30 and we knew it wouldn’t be the cleanest game. We knew O’Dowd would get back into the game. We got off to a good start, which was great to see after falling behind in some games before the break,” said coach Bryan Gardere. It was another phenomenal game for senior guard Natalia Martinez who finished with 41 points. It was the sixth time she had scored at least 40 points in a game this season. “Honestly, my finishing wasn’t the best, but we’ll take the win,” said Martinez. “We’re just going to keep focusing on improving. At the end of the day, this was Photos by Eric Taylor Natalia Martinez scored 41 points against Bishop O’Dowd, her sixth 40-point game of the season. just one game and we have many more to worry about.” Piedmont’s recreation department hosted family night at the game against O’Dowd, and kids were lined up to get Martinez’s autograph. Lindsey Wirgler is playing with a mask after getting hit on the nose in a previous game. She scored a season-high 22 points against St. Joseph. “It’s great. I was that little kid not so long ago. To be able to give back to this community after Piedmont has given so much to us, it’s the bare minimum,” said Martinez. “The last player to do anything close to this was Courtney Paris. It’s incredible. We’re seeing history before our eyes. But I’m not surprised. Natalia has put a lot into this,” said Gardere. 59-50 over Bishop O’Dowd Piedmont held the Dragons to just four points in the first quarter and shocked the Dragons with an early, huge lead of 18-4. O’Dowd clawed back, but still trailed Piedmont 30-16 at halftime and 42-28 entering the fourth quarter. PHS defense dominated the first quarter by limiting O’Dowd to just two baskets. Martinez scored 13 of the Highlanders’ 18 points, and put up 10 of Piedmont’s 12 points in the second quarter. Final stats: Martinez scored 41 points, Lindsey Wirgler scored nine, Shakila Zuberi had six, Sam Smith had two and Kat Melian had one. Shakila Zuberi lines up a 3-pointer against Bishop O’Dowd.
articles.title: Piedmont girls beat Bishop O’Dowd 59-50

articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team wrapped up a solid week with two wins and a loss in their last three games. After losing by 20 points to Western Alameda County Conference foe Alameda, 58-38, on Wednesday, January 10 at home, they followed up with a 58-47 league win over St. Joseph on the road and pulled out a 2-point victory over former state champion Fremont of Oakland, 48-46, in the MLK Showcase at Merritt College on Monday, January 15. Piedmont twice held double-digit leads against Fremont before the Tigers went on scoring runs in the third and fourth quarters. Piedmont had to overcome 25 turnovers to achieve its victory. “Fremont is a really long and athletic team. Doing film-study, we knew they had players who could score with the best of them. I think we did a good job shutting down their best player” said coach Ben Spencer. “It’s hard to win games [like that], but we never gave up the lead.” Senior forward Brit Burden led with 26 points against Fremont and had a big week with 16 points against Alameda and 24 against St. Joseph. Burden has shown improvement in each appearance with his ability to finish at the rim and draw fouls. “I’ve been working on my preparation before games and that’s translating. You just have to control getting to the hoop and finishing,” said Burden. Spencer is seeing how Burden can take control of games. He had a huge block to end the game. “He’s figured out after the Novato game that he’s going to be the best player on the floor offensively and defensively. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team remained undefeated season with 3-0 wins over Mt. Eden on Friday, January 12, and San Lorenzo two days earlier. Both matches were played at Chabot College in Hayward. The pair of games brings the Highlanders’ record to 6-1-0 overall (W-T-L) and 1-1-0 against Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division opponents after tying 2-2 with Castro Valley the previous week. “We threw it away against Castro Valley after being up 2-0 with 10 minutes to go. But I like our response since then, I think our intensity is great and we’re working really hard on the defensive end,” said coach Todd Sullivan. “We have a solid group of 11 and know our set-team now. It’s a case of the players getting more comfortable with each other and understanding each other’s game,” The Highlanders scored all three goals against Mt. Eden in the first half, and piled on two second-half goals against the Grizzlies of San Lorenzo. “I think we’re getting stronger. In the early portion of the schedule, we were struggling to finish. In the first half [against Mt. Eden], we were doing a great job at finishing and connecting passes. The game got chippy in the second half, but we managed to keep the clean sheet, so shoutout to our defenders,” said Bosco Lorin, who scored two goals and an assist against Mt. Eden. Piedmont looks ahead to a critical week of league matches on the road. They face San Leandro tonight, January 17, play at Bishop O’Dowd on Friday, and face Berkeley on Tuesday, January 23. The Dragons are currently 8-1-1 and the Yellowjackets are 11-0-1. “One of our strengths has been playing together and I think that’s how we’ve pulled a lot of our results. That’s going to be important as we transition into the latter part of the season,” said captain Riley Stratman. “We just need to keep practicing, stay sharp, and stay healthy. We need to treat these upcoming games like we’ve treated the rest of these teams. They are tough teams, but we’re a strong team, too. articles.text: Staff Photos Miranda Liu (left) and Elsa Wallway celebrate Wallway’s first goal against Alameda. Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team posted a 2-2 draw with Alameda on the road on Thursday, January 11, but lost 3-0 to Castro Valley at Chabot College two days earlier. The results bring its record to 6-1-1 (0-1-1 in league). Returning from Winter Break means the Highlanders are getting several players back from their club schedule, including sophomore striker Miranda Liu, the Post’s Freshman of the Year in 2023. “I think we were good enough to win [against Alameda], I though they did well. It’s always tough to come to Thompson Field (slick and bumpy), and we dealt with it fairly well. It’s obviously great to bring back strong players from their club teams. I thought we had a good second-half against Castro Valley,” said coach Dan Chubbock. The Highlanders initially led 1-0 over Alameda before allowing a goal prior to halftime and another in the 52nd minute. But Piedmont tied the match in the 70th minute but couldn’t find the back of the net for a game-winner. “Coming into the season is always a big shock because we all are coming from our club teams and we have to gel in just a week or two. The early portion of the schedule is always tough, so now it’s just trying to mesh and became as cohesive as we can,” said senior Lola Beihn. Both Piedmont goals were scored by freshman Elsa Wallway in an impressive varsity debut. She played the club season with the De Anza Force. “Miranda had a great assist on the first goal and I was just able to slip it behind their defense into the net. The second half goal was a great press out of the back. It honestly feels great and I feel super fortunate to play with these girls and this team,” said Wallway. 2-2 draw with Alameda Piedmont had a couple of shots on target in the first half prior to the first goal with Julianna Miranda Liu with a chip shot goal attempt against Alameda.

articles.text: Editor: On the week of January 15-22, Piedmont Key Club will be running a soccer equipment drive at Piedmont High and Piedmont Middle School, and Havens Elementary. This drive is for any type of soccer equipment, from balls to cleats, shin guards, and even athletic clothing. Donations will go to the charity, Soccer Without Borders, an organization that reaches out to students and kids in the community through soccer. They focus especially on making a space for newcomer youth (refugees and immigrants) to connect with their peers and community by providing resources and training for soccer teams. together and help children develop social and developmental skills through the sport of soccer. Look for the donation bins and posters throughout the PHS, PMS, and Havens campuses. –Sabrina Olliphant PHS Key Club president

articles.text: With an enrollment size typically around 900 students, you will often see recurring faces at Witter Field, Binks Rawlings Gym, Humphries Diamond, and Witter Softball Field. Here is a feature-piece on three influential athletes at the school who are competing in multiple sports. OLIVER SHAFROTH Soccer & Lacrosse MARKOS LAGIOS Football & Baseball Junior Markos Lagios is the football team’s starting quarterback and will be entering his third year as a starter on the baseball team this spring. He recently was named as a second-team AllMetro selection by the San Francisco Chronicle. Last fall, Lagios led the Highlanders to a 7-4 record and a berth in the North Coast Section playoffs. It was the school’s first league title since 2015. In 2023, Lagios completed 62 percent of his passes in 2023 for 1,941 passing yards, 22 touchdowns and just three interceptions. Lagios also ran for 788 rushing yards, averaging over five yards per carry, and added 13 more touchdowns to his tally, giving him 35 total scores. In baseball Lagios plays both centerfield and third base, Last year he hit for a .303 average with 23 hits, 11 doubles, three triples, 18 RBIs and led the team with two home runs and 27 runs scored. The Highlanders went 14-11 last spring after being bumped up to the WACC’s Foothill Division. They reached the NCS Semifinals as the No. 8 seed and upset No. 1 Fortuna 5-2 in the quarterfinals and beating No. 9 Branson 4-3 in a 12-inning opening round win. Photo by Todd Marshburn Hailey Marshburn is a four-year starter on both the soccer and lacrosse varsity teams. Oliver Shafroth, a senior utility player on the soccer team is also a former first-team AllLeague recipient on the lacrosse team. He has appeared as a midfielder and a defender in coach Todd Sullivan’s soccer lineup, making a difference with his strength, comparable to former player Jack Nelson. Shafroth will be entering his third year on the varsity lacrosse team. He led the team last season as their primary faceoff specialist, and helped lead them to their sixth consecutive league championship in 2023. He recorded one assist and dominated the faceoff circle in Piedmont’s 14-6 win over Bishop O’Dowd in the title game by claiming 12 face-offs. Piedmont finished last year with a 14-4 record and reached HAILEY MARSHBURN Soccer & Lacrosse Hailey Marshburn wears the captain’s armband for the girls’ soccer team this winter. She plays midfield and also has the speed to move out wide as a fullback. Marshburn has scored once so far this season, Last year, she scored the game-winning goal in Piedmont’s sudden-death 2-1 win over No. 1 seed University to claim the North Coast Section title. Marshburn is a four-year starter on the lacrosse team and was often tasked to move the ball upfield with her speed and elusiveness. She was among Piedmont’s leaders in ground ball recoveries. articles.text: Piedmont High School’s Sailing Club is getting ready for its season starting February 3, with an introductory clinic the week before, on Sunday, January 28. As part of the Encinal Yacht Club High School Sailing Program, participants attend regular practices at the yacht club in Alameda and will be in several weekend regattas in the Bay Area and Southern California. The regattas are organized by the Pacific Coast Interscholastic Sailing Association (PCISA). Sophie Hess, a Piedmont High junior, joined the team in the fall. “I have loved being on the sailing team because it’s a great way to take advantage of the opportunity to actually sail pretty close to home. It is amazing to go to school then drive to Alameda, rig a boat and enjoy a gorgeous sunset from the water. It is an amazing experience. As a beginner to sailing, I felt a bit intimidated; but everyone has been so welcoming and friendly.” PHS senior Peter Stokes joined the team as a sophomore. “Small boat sailing is the most involved and fun type of sailing, it can be as competitive as you want it to be and offers a great way to meet people from other schools in the Bay,” he said. Team captain Mica Jorcino, a senior, joined the EYC high school sailing program as an 8th grader and is currently hoping to continue sailing in college. “I’ve been able to learn so many new skills and have gained so much knowledge as I get out of my comfort zone. It’s a super welcoming environment and I have loved seeing our team grow with so many people and incredible coaches these past five years,” she said. For more information reach out to Mica Jorcino at 24micaelajo@piedmont.k12.ca.us, or visit tinyurl.com/PHSsailing. Photos by Sophie Hess Mica Jorcino and Peter Stokes, PHS Seniors, at the NorCal regatta in the San Francisco Bay off of Richmond. The Encinal Yacht Club Jr. Sailing Program works in partnership with a number of East Bay high schools who have teams or clubs that participate in the Interscholastic Sailing Association.

pages.text: Wednesday, January 17, 2024 15 HIKING WITH JON By Jonathan Comeaux The rains from earlier this month have tapered off, but the impact can be seen in flowing streams and creeks. Winter hiking is the best time to visit the local waterfalls, and the Post has ventured to several in the Bay Area. Here’s a collection of local waterfalls to see: Uvas Canyon’s Waterfalls Loop Trail, Morgan Hill In Morgan Hill’s Uvas Canyon County Park are a collection of five accessible waterfalls in 5.2 miles of total hiking. Waterfall hikes to consider You’ll still require 1,273 feet in elevation gain to see all five in the entire loop—but four of those waterfalls within the first 1.6 miles—making the last long trip to Triple Falls, and optional excursion if you’re worried about tired legs. Cataract Creek, Mt. Tamalpais Watershed The Cataract Falls Trail in the Mt. Tamalpais Watershed is a 4.8 out-and-back with around 1,000 feet in elevation gain. There are two trailheads, parking on Bolinas Fairfax Road will provide just a 0.5 walk to the first waterfall and another 0.2 to its most famous Helen Markt Falls. Should you walk the entire Cataract Falls Trail, you will encounter cascades along cataract creek. Murietta Falls, Del Valle Regional Wilderness Murietta Falls in Livermore’s Del Valle Regional Park is considered the highest waterfall in the entire Bay Area at an elevation of near 3,000 feet in the Ohlone Wilderness, where a small stream cascades over 100 foot cliff-face – meaning this location should only be taken by experienced hikers looking for a challenge. Staff Photo You can see Helen Markt Falls in 0.7 miles of hiking in the Mt. Tamalpais Watershed along Cataract Creek. Alamere Falls is thriving and currently is its most active in several years. Photo courtesy of AllTrails SPRING SEASON 2024 JAN 22ND-MAY 10TH SKYLINE LACROSSE Join the Journey to Greatness REGISTER www.skylinelacrosse.com GIRLS AGES 7-14 Staff Photo Uvas Canyon County Park has five waterfalls to enjoy, including four in the first 1.5 miles. Photo courtesy of AllTrails The waterfall at Murietta Falls in the Dal Valle Regional Wilderness is thriving after snow touched down in the area in late December. Photos courtesy of AllTrails Dawn Falls in Mt. Tamalpais can be seen in just 1.5 miles of hiking. The entire day required 12.1 miles of hiking and near 5,000 feet in elevation gain; it is considered a good training spot for those interested in Half Dome. Alamere Falls, Point Reyes National Seashore The trek to Alamere Falls is a total of 13.6 miles and an elevation gain of 1,811 feet taking the Coastal Trail to the Wildcat Campground. There is a shortcut at 4.5 miles, but it requires scrambling down a steep ravine to the beach and should only be done by experienced hikers who are comfortable with scrambling. Proper footwear is needed. Dawn Falls, Mt. Tamalpais We visited Dawn Falls in November, and it was a trickle off a large cliff-face. But fellow hikers online describe that its intensity picked up after the rain in the winter months. The walk to the location takes just 1.4 miles at around 500 feet in elevation gain through lush redwoods. The walk is popular and we passed 49 people in the trek to Dawn Falls.

articles.text: Sin Wai Kin and Gabriel Chaile exhibits on view As part of MATRIX, an exhibition series that provides artists with an experimental platform to make and show new work, the internationally recognized visual artists Sin Wai Kin and Gabriel Chaile have opened their first U.S. solo exhibitions at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA). Best known for category-defying performances and moving image works, Sin will present new work in MATRIX 284 / Sin Wai Kin: The Story Changing. In addition to a recent video work, Dreaming the End (2023), Sin’s six-channel video work The Breaking Story (2022) will spill out from the galleries and into the museum’s public space. The Toronto-born artist draws on references ranging from Cantonese and Peking opera to early performances in London’s experimental drag scene, in which their popular onstage persona pastiched an idealized version of Western femininity. Since then, the artist’s view has grown to encompass an expanding universe of characters who explore how social narratives are understood and transformed. Sin’s MATRIX exhibition will remain on view at BAMPFA through March 10, 2024. MATRIX 283 / Gabriel Chaile: No hay nada que destruya el corazón como la pobreza centers upon Chaile’s large-scale sculptural commission, which he completed onsite in collaboration with the UC Berkeley Art Practice department during a residency preceding the exhibition. Born in San Miguel de Tucumán, the Lisbon-based artist Gabriel Chaile, Rosario Liendro, 2022. In the artists’ first U.S. solo exhibitions, the works of Chaile and Sin Wai Kin are on view at Berkeley art Museum. has been celebrated worldwide — including at the 59th Venice Biennale last year — for his soaring, anthropomorphic clay sculptures that expand on the forms, rituals and traditions of pre-colonial cultures in his native Argentina. Chaile’s practice intertwines indigenous mythology and contemporary social and political references, including Tucumán Arde (Tucumán is Burning), a series of “happenings” by the artist that expose the region’s widespread poverty from the 1960s onward, following the federal government’s closure of key sugar mills. Chaile’s MATRIX exhibition, the title of which translates to “Nothing destroys the heart like poverty,” will remain on view at BAMPFA through April 14, 2024. The museum is located at 2155 Center Street and is open from 11 a.m. through 7 p.m., Wednesday through Sunday. Tickets ($14 general admission) and more details are available at bampfa. org, or walk-up at the museum desk.

articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO) will celebrate its 87th season with its Winter Concert on Saturday, January 27 at Walnut Creek Presbyterian Church at 7:30 p.m. This year’s event marks Maestro David Ramadanoff’s 34th season as Music Director/Conductor, and features an inaugural collaboration with a longstanding Bay Area institution, the Berkeley Community Chorus and Orchestra (BCCO). The two groups will feature BCCO classical soprano singer Vuyiswa Sigadi and solo violinist Henry Stroud, the YPSO concertmaster, a sophomore at Berkeley High School and the winner of this season’s YPSO concerto competition. The concert opens with American composer Kenji Bunch’s Supermaximum — a contemporary composition that explores themes of resilience and determination. According to Bunch, “this body of work serves as a singular example of a group of oppressed people resorting to, of all things, art for spiritual and, at times, physical survival under the most needlessly cruel of circumstances.” Following this, YPSO will perform the first movement of Camille Saint-Saëns’ Violin Concerto No. 3 in B Minor, Op. 61. According to program notes writer Orrin Howard, the violin concerto’s “first movement revolves around a bold, dramatic first theme, a songful contrasting theme, and fistsful of rapid scales, arpeggios, and double stops.” Closing the program is Poulenc’s Gloria, a choral and orchestral masterpiece that reflects the composer’s unique blend of sacred and secular influences. Poulenc’s Gloria is a joyous and vibrant work, featuring lush harmonies and intricate textures. The orchestra and chorus will be led by Ming Luke, BCCO Music Director. Founded in Berkeley in 1936, YPSO is the oldest youth orchestra in California and the first independent youth orchestra in the nation. YPSO’s mission is to “encourage young people to become exemplary musicians and young musicians to become exemplary people”. The organization presents four regular concerts per season. In addition, they reach out through programs such as Bread and Roses and the Bay Area Music Project to bring music into the lives of the surrounding community and encourage the civic development of its students. Tickets ($20-$30) for the event at Walnut Creek Presbyterian Church (1801 Lacassie Avenue) are available online at ypsomusic. org/tickets. Young People’s Symphony Orchestra will celebrate its Winter Concert on Saturday, January 27, marking its 87th season and inaugural collaboration with the Berkeley Community Chorus and Orchestra. articles.text: Lineup includes stand-up comics, actors, improv troupes SF Sketchfest begins tomorrow, marking the return of the Bay Area’s largest annual comedy festival. From January 18 through February 4, audiences can watch prominent stand-up comedians Maria Bamford, Marc Maron, Joel Kim, Matt Braunger and others perform alongside local comedians and celebrity guests like Bob Odenkirk, Weird Al Yankovic, and Eric Idle of Monty Python’s Flying Circus in a variety of stand-up shows, live podcasts, variety shows, and musical performances. This year’s festival boasts more than 175 comedy shows across 17 different venues in the city. A full lineup is available online at www.sfsketchfest.com. SF Sketchfest was founded in 2001 by Bay Area comics David Owen, Cole Stratton, and Janet Varney as a way to showcase the talents of Bay Area sketch comedy groups. Since its inception, the event has grown rapidly into a nationally recognized comedy festival that mixes national headliners, local favorites, and the best up-and-coming groups from throughout North America for nearly a month of sketch, improv, stand-up, and alternative comedy. Tickets are available online at www.sfsketchfest.com. Sold-out shows may still have a limited number of tickets available at the venue’s box office the night of the show. A line begins approximately 60-90 minutes before showtime, and any available seats will be sold on a first-come, firstserved basis. Photo by SF Sketchfest This year’s festival boasts more than 175 comedy shows across 17 different venues around the city.

articles.text: Multiple Grammy nominee R&B singer-songwriter Terry Steele performs a concert this Sunday, January 21 at 7 p.m. at Yoshi’s in Oakland. The music reflects the legacy of singer-songwriting Luther Vandross, alongside special tributes to Whitney Houston and Aretha Franklin. Steele, a two-time American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishing (ASCAP) Award Winning Songwriter, has toured internationally for decades as a professional recording artist, with concert performances in Russia, Japan, China, Germany, Brazil, Jamaica, Israel, England and all throughout the U.S. As a songwriter, Steele has written for or collaborated with artists as Whitney Houston, Dionne Warwick, Starship, Hiroshima, Patti Labelle, Stevie Wonder, Diana Ross, The Spinners, Barry White, The Pointer Sisters, Arif Mardin, Natalie Cole, George Duke and saxophonist Richard Elliott. As the principal writer of the blockbuster hit, Here And Now, (recorded by the late Vandross), Steele won a Grammy nomination for “Best Rhythm and Blues Song” in 1990. Separate concert on January 23 Two days later, on Tuesday, January 23 at 8 p.m., multiple Grammy nominee, Guggenheim Fellow and MacArthur Fellow Terry Steele will perform at Yoshi’s this Sunday, January 21, and the Miguel Zenón Quartet, pictured, will take the stage on Tuesday, January 23. Miguel Zenón performs with his jazz quartet as one of the most groundbreaking and influential saxophonists and composers of his generation. Born and raised in San Juan, Puerto Rico, Zenón has released fifteen recordings as a jazz leader, including the Grammy nominated El Arte Del Bolero (2021). As a composer he has been commissioned by SFJAZZ, NYO Jazz, The New York State Council for the Arts, Chamber Music America, Logan Center for The Arts, The Hyde Park Jazz Festival, The John Simon Guggenheim Foundation, MIT, Spektral Quartet, The Hewlett Foundation, Peak Performances, PRISM Quartet and many of his peers. In addition, Zenón topped both the Jazz Artist of the Year and Alto Saxophonist categories on the 2014 Jazz Times Critics Poll and was selected as the Alto Saxophonist of the Year by the Jazz Journalist Association in 2015, 2018, 2019 and 2020 (when he was also recognized as Arranger of the Year). Doors for each show at Yoshi’s (510 Embarcadero West) open half an hour in advance. Tickets ($35-$69 for Terry Steele, $29- $69 for Miguel Zenón Quartet) and more details are available at yoshis.com.
articles.title: Terry Steele, Miguel Zenón Quartet coming to Yoshi’s

articles.text: The Diluvian String Quartet will perform their winter recital, Love Notes. at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, February 9 at 7 p.m. The public is invited to come and enjoy a romantic Valentine’s recital. Oozing with passion (and cheese), the program will include Germaine Tailleferre’s debut String Quartet, Robert Schumann’s most famous 3rd String Quartet, and other works by Mozart and Webern. Doors Open at 6:45 p.m. Tickets are $20 and are available online at Eventbrite or at the door. A dessert reception and drinks will follow the concert. The quartet includes Elizabeth Castro Greenberg and Jessica Scrimale, violin, Raphael Gold, viola, and Sylvia Woodmansee, cello. This will be their fifth appearance in Piedmont and will be another fun and diverse musical journey. On the program is Mozart’s Adagio and Fugue in C minor, a short, profound score that Mozart adapted from an earlier work for 2 pianos. This piece, written toward the end of Mozart’s life, was a tribute to the baroque era, and has entertained audiences since the late 18th century. Germaine Tailleferre was the only female member of the group of “les 6”, a group of French composers forging a new voice in the early 20th century. In this quartet, we can hear her fresh, humorous voice, written over the course of 2 years and published in 1919 at the end of the Great War. A superb talent, her music is sadly not heard often enough. Anton von Webern’s Langsamer Satz, or slow movement, written in 1905, is said to have been written as a sort of love letter to his future wife following a hike. Intended to be part of a full length string quartet, this piece is no doubt a short musical journey through the joys and fears of young love. Robert Schumann’s third quartet, his last and perhaps most famous, begins with two notes and is said to be a musical way of saying his wife’s name, Clara. Always lyrical, tonally lush, and beautiful, it is a work not to be missed. The Diluvian String Quartet – Elizabeth Castro Greenberg and Jessica Scrimale, violin, Raphael Gold, viola, and Sylvia Woodmansee, cello – will perform a Valentine concert in Piedmont on Saturday evening, February 9.
articles.title: Love Notes Diluvian Quartet concert at PCA on Feb. 9

articles.text: The chamber quartet Ives Collective comes to Old First Presbyterian Church in San Francisco for a hybrid, in-person, and livestreamed concert on Sunday, January 28 at 4 p.m. The quartet – comprised of violinist Kay Stern, violinist and violist Susan Freier, cellist Stephen Harrison and pianist Elizabeth Schumann – will play Mélanie Bonis’ Soir et Matin for Piano Trio, Op. 76; Dame Ethyl Smyth’s String Trio in D Major, Op. 6; and Bonis’ Piano Quartet No. 1 in B-flat major, Op. 69. Presenting powerful live music through fresh and informed interpretations of established masterworks and under-appreciated gems, the quartet continues its commitment to presenting lesser heard works by women composers. Program notes The composer Bonis just missed studying at the Paris Conservatoire under Fauré. Like many talented women of her time, her parents discouraged her studies, forcing her to drop out as soon as she became engaged. It wasn’t until 1891 that she was recognized through a musical competition, one that she entered The chamber quartet Ives Collective comes to Old First Presbyterian Church for a hybrid concert on January 28. under the name M. Bonis. The jury awarded her first prize, initially mistaking her for a man. Piano Quartet in B-flat major, Op. 69 is a wonderful example of Bonis’ feel for melody and atmosphere. Dame Ethel Smyth, born in 1858 like Bonis, nevertheless led a very different life from her French contemporary. She was an avid member of the women’s suffrage movement. Despite suffering the same bigotry toward her work that plagued other female composers – her father was very much opposed to her work – she became the first female composer to be granted a damehood. Her ambitious String Trio, like so much of her chamber music, has only recently been resurrected. The Ives Collective was formed in 2015 by Co-Artistic Directors Susan Freier and Stephen Harrison following the disbanding of their group under the name Ives Quartet. The music background of the musicians includes San Francisco Symphony, San Francisco Opera, San Francisco Ballet Orchestra, San Francisco Chamber Orchestra, the Metropolitan Opera, Opera Parallèle and many university faculties and festivals. Tickets ($25 in-person general admission; $20 suggested donation for online live-stream) for the concert at Old First Presbyterian Church (1751 Sacramento St.) are available at oldfirstconcerts.org, or by phone at 415-474-1608.
articles.title: Ives Collective at Old First Presbyterian on Jan. 28

articles.text: World Harmony Chorus will present a free vocal concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Tuesday January 30 at 7:30 p.m. Audience members will enjoy hearing songs from Brazil, Ukraine, Galicia, Kenya, Korea, and Iceland. Hear stunning a cappella arrangements of traditional songs that feature unique musical traditions, unfamiliar languages and polyrhythms. Bring friends who like to sing and stay for refreshments. World Harmony Chorus is a community chorus that welcomes participants of all ages and ability levels. At our Friends & Family Concerts, we perform our current repertoire and then invite the entire audience to join us in learning and singing a couple of new songs. No singing experience is required. Tryouts on February 13 Try a free choral tryout on February 13 at 7:00 p.m. then join weekly rehearsals on Tuesday evenings. No auditions are needed; just show up at the first rehearsal at Berkeley Shambhala Center, 2288 Fulton Street, #203, in Berkeley. Singers at all levels are welcome! Director Betsy Blakeslee has directed choruses in multiple countries. Arranger Daniel Steinberg is one of the foremost a cappella world music arrangers. ®
articles.title: World Harmony Choral concert at Center for the Arts

Germaine Tailleferre was the only female member of the group of “les 6”, a group of French composers forging a new voice in the early 20th century. In this quartet, we can hear her fresh, humorous voice, written over the course of 2 years and published in 1919 at the end of the Great War. A superb talent, her music is sadly not heard often enough. Anton von Webern’s Langsamer Satz, or slow movement, written in 1905, is said to have been written as a sort of love letter to his future wife following a hike. Intended to be part of a full length string quartet, this piece is no doubt a short musical journey through the joys and fears of young love. Robert Schumann’s third quartet, his last and perhaps most famous, begins with two notes and is said to be a musical way of saying his wife’s name, Clara. Always lyrical, tonally lush, and beautiful, it is a work not to be missed. articles.text: Sick children doing daily battle with debilitating and potentially lethal diseases turns the word entertainment on its head. And yet it is a theme that’s familiar in Hollywood. Extraordinary Measures is about a rare affliction known as Pompe’s Disease, a form of muscular dystrophy that strikes children at an early age, all too often truncating their young lives; most don’t live to be older than eight or nine years. The symptoms are enlarged organs and muscles that atrophy to the point where they can’t lift an arm to throw a small ball. It has to do with a missing enzyme that converts sugar in their muscles. Imagine the agony of those parents who watch their children slowly say goodbye, growing weaker and less resilient as months and then years pass and time grows ever shorter and symptoms become increasingly life threatening. The film Extraordinary Measures is based on the true story of a father and mother, John and Aileen Crowley (Brendan Fraser and Keri Russell), who refuse to quietly say goodbye to their son and daughter who are both afflicted with Pompe’s Disease. John, after reading all the literature, desperate for any possible breakthrough, sets out in search of a research scientist, Doctor Robert Stonehill (Harrison Ford), who is doing groundbreaking work regarding enzymes. He is also perpetually cranky and under-funded. As Crowley, a Harvard MBA, finds high finance money, Stonehill concentrates on the cure. The game clock, sadly, is ticking for the Crowley children who are both in crisis. Time is of the essence. Surprisingly, the weakest part of Extraordinary Measures is the portrayal of Stonehill by Ford. Scientists, of course, can be eccentric and reclusive; however, if they’re likable and seem to have a good heart, well, that is redemptive. But if they’re self-absorbed, selfish and uncaring, then they’re decidedly unattractive. Sadly and surprisingly, Stonehill is the latter. Ford’s performance reminds viewers that he often plays someone who is short-tempered, out of sorts and verging on anger (all without a sense of humor, a quality that often saves Bruce Willis as he plays Bruce Willis over and over again). Ford is a huge movie star and someone who audiences clearly enjoy spending time with. In this film, however, he is miscast. The partnership between the parents and Stonehill is never satisfactory. Instead Stonehill finds the parents and his fellow scientists intrusive and a distraction and too often becomes petulant – not endearing qualities. They detract from the film consistently, until the end of act three when Stonehill softens, but by then it’s too late. Extraordinary Measures. Directed by Tom Vaughn. Starring Harrison Ford, Brendan Fraser and Keri Russell. 1 jr., 46 min. Rated PG. Released 2010, Now streaming on VUDU/prime/ apple tv. articles.text: Saoirse Ronan stas in The Lovely Bones The film The Lovely Bones, based on Alice Sebold’s bestselling book, immediately lets the audience know two things: Susie Salmon (Saoirse Ronan), a 14-year-old, is murdered, and the man who lures her into an underground room where he rapes and kills her is a seemingly a benign neighbor, George Harvey played by Stanley Tucci. The question that Susie asks after this horrific event in a haunting voiceover, is, “Will there be justice? Will Harvey, a serial predator, be found out?” Sebold uses a familiar narrative device: Susie, a lovely, quintessential teen, now dead, is trapped in an incandescent purgatory, a morphing place called “the in-between.” And it’s from that vantage point she watches her parents cope with the loss of their beloved daughter. Both are devastated, mired in a wrenching grief, and relentlessly pushing the case detective who has no leads or suspects. The film is predicated on a reality that no parent ever wants to encounter, which is that beneath the patina of societal civility resides an unadorned evil and a pathology that is incomprehensible. Predators are ever with us. And our children, hobbled by their inherent innocence, cannot be completely protected. Had director Peter Jackson explored that truth without dressing the film up with an over-thetop psychedelic view of “the in-between,” The Lovely Bones would have been a far edgier and engaging film. articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Saban’s Power Rangers is an unabashed movie for older kids and teens with lots of CGI action and other wild, over-the-top stuff that kids will really like. Personally, I’m a sucker for origin films and the first act (plus part of act two) is a good one. You have five kids who all look like they are on the Student Council, but somehow end up in detention (think the Breakfast Club). Each one feels powerless and definitely misunderstood until they aren’t, which doesn’t happen until well into act three. But therein is the real story of The Power Rangers and all other comic book movies that take wimpy kids and give them super powers. What adolescent doesn’t wish he or she had some serious mojo? You can start with Spiderman and go through the deep Marvel and DC Comics bench and it’s all about power and how it’s used. Kids love this idea. It’s brilliant. In Power Rangers, you have five young people who are given the gift (just the way that Harry Potter was) and now it’s up to them to make use of it. Of course, act two and three of this nostalgic reboot, based on a 1993 TV series, get nuts with Naomi Watts showing up as ultracampy Rita Repulsa, who is evil incarnate and wants to lay waste to all, including the bucolic town’s Krispy Kreme donut shop. Really. But here’s the deal: Rangers is all about friendship, bonding, and finally morphing. It’s also got a quirky robot named Alpha 5, portrayed by Bill Hader, as well as a very cool space ship buried deep in a quarry. The kids could have gone back to school and hassled some bullies (one does get his mild comeuppance), but they have bigger things to do. Like save their families and their town. This is a popcorn movie. But a good one for kids and even their parents. Saban’s Power Rangers. Directed by Dean Iaraelite. Starring Dacre Montgomery, Naomi Scott and RJ Cryer. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2017. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv. Saban’s Power Rangers trilogy. M I C H A E L
