articles.text: Survey of Retro and Mid-Century Jewelry by Sacha Grippando Sacha Grippando will present a lecture at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on February 1 at 6 p.m. featuring the jewelry collection of American actress Elizabeth Taylor. Jewelry from the 1930s–1960s is bold, colorful and extravagant. Elizabeth Taylor and the Duchess of Windsor amassed what are considered today to be the best collections of jewelry from the 20th century. They both had amazing taste and a passion for important gemstones and innovative and avant-garde design. As the majority of their collections were acquired as gifts from their husbands, these collections are truly legacies of love. Both women led extraordinary lives that were very public. They were often vilified, criticized and at certain points in their lives portrayed as “the most hated women in the world” by the press. This pair of lectures will focus on jewelry from these two collections from the 1930s to the 1960s, as both feature the best of the best from this time period, and will include gorgeous photos and discussions on some of their most important pieces of jewelry from the ‘30s to the ‘60s, along with fascinating stories about these women and their controversial lives. The February 1 lecture explores the collection of Elizabeth Taylor, who shared the Duchess’ love of jewelry and also has some of the best examples from the 1950s-60s. Her collection was also the result of gifts from her husbands, predominantly from Mike Todd and Richard Burton. It was not until later in her life that she purchased pieces on her own, her first being the Prince of Wales brooch that had belonged to the Duchess of Windsor. She purchased it from the Duke and Duchess of Windsor sale at Sotheby’s in 1987. Taylor’s collection was considered the best collection of important gemstones and jewelry in the world. She was an ardent admirer and collector of pieces from Bulgari, the Italian jewelry firm that came to the forefront during this period, helped greatly by her purchases and her very public wearing of their finest pieces. She was also a collector of famous gemstones like the 33.19 ct. Krupp diamond, the 68 ct. Taylor-Burton diamond and the 16th-century pear- shaped pearl, famously known as La Peregrina, that was once owned by King Philip II of Spain (1527-1598). Continuing her illustrated Lecture Series exploring the Jewelry Arts: Sacha Grippando Gemologist

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse is ringing in 2024 with the world premiere of playwright Minna Lee’s My Home on the Moon from January 25 through February 24. In this epic sci-fi journey into the metaverse, business is booming for a formerly failing Vietnamese pho restaurant in the middle of a gentrified neighborhood after it receives help from a mysterious marketing consultant. Things are not all they seem as the restaurant’s waiter, Mai, discovers that artificial intelligence-powered simulations may be taking over reality. With the help of her friends and family, and armed with delicious pho, Mai must learn to reckon the perfection of artificial life with the welcome imperfection of reality. A finalist in the 2024 Bay Area Playwrights Festival and semi-finalist at Ashland New Plays Festival, My Home on the Moon received developmental readings at UC Santa Cruz’s Rainbow Theater Festival and Denver, Colorado-based arts collective Bucharest Inside the Beltway. For tickets ($15-$100) and more information about the performance at SF Playhouse (450 Post Street), visit sfplayhouse.org or call the box office at 415-677-9596 Marketing consultant Vera (Rinabeth Apostol) learns the art of cooking pho from Mai (Jenny Nguyen Nelson) in the world premiere of My Home on the Moon at San Francisco Playhouse January 25 through February 24.

articles.text: The Lesher Center for the Arts Repertory Company opens its 2024 season with the remarkable hit solo show, Every Brilliant Thing, on view through January 28. Making a list of things that make life worth living would get different responses from different people, and what would be at the top? Family? Ice cream? The even-numbered Star Trek films? For the lead character in this uplifting play, it’s his mother. This surprising and immersive theatrical experience by Duncan Macmillan and Jonny Donahoe delves into the human experience with playfulness and love. With poignant humor and joy, Every Brilliant Thing takes audiences on a journey through favorite moments such as falling in love, as well as grief, healing, and discovering and rediscovering all that life has to give. Directed by celebrated Bay Area fixture Jeffrey Lo and starring Oakland Theater Project Co-Artistic Director William Thomas Hodgson, the story is filled with opportunities for warm, fun audience participation. The show premiered at the Ludlow Fringe Festival, then it was performed off Broadway at Barrow Street Theatre where it was filmed for HBO. It was deemed a “heart-wrenching, hilarious play” by The Guardian; The New York Times called it “captivating.” Time Out London lauded the work as “gloriously funny and exceptionally warm,” while The Independent said it “finds a perfect balance between conveying the struggles of life, and celebrating all that is sweet in it.” For tickets ($35-$40) visit LesherArtsCenter.org or call the box office at (925) 943-7469. Lesher Center for the Arts is located at 1601 Civic Drive in Walnut Creek. William Thomas Hodgson stars in Every Brilliant Thing at the Lesher Center for the Arts in Walnut Creek through January 28.
articles.title: See Every Brilliant Thing at Lesher Center through Jan. 28

articles.text: Cult of Love will be performed by Berkeley Repertory Theatre from January 26 through March 3. Cult of Love, written by Leslye Headland and directed by Trip Cullman, will open at Berkeley Repertory Theatre on Friday, January 26, for a five-week run. Cult of Love is a ruthless comedy about a deeply Christian family, the Dahls, devoted to their belief that all one needs is love. The four Dahl siblings were brought up with a devotion to Jesus and each other. Now adults with their own distinct beliefs and years of emotional wariness, they gather once again for the holidays at their childhood home, singing joyous carols and recreate family traditions. However, repressed feelings and conflicts about the siblings’ upbringing shatter the family’s façade of forced cheer, and all hell soon breaks loose. Bold and provocative, Cult of Love dares to challenge our perceptions of family to examine what’s truly needed for deep faith and love to persist. “All families are inherently complicated, but in Leslye Headland and Trip Cullman’s hands, they are also dynamic, dramatic, and wildly entertaining,” said Berkeley Rep Artistic Director Johanna Pfaelzer. “I’m delighted to welcome this incredibly gifted cast and creative team to Berkeley Rep.” Tickets ($22.50–$134) may be purchased at the box office or online at berkeleyrep.org/shows/ cult-of-love, or by phone at 647- 2949. Berkeley Rep’s Roda Theater is located at 2015 Addison Street.
articles.title: Cult of Love opens at Berkeley Rep Jan. 26

articles.text: La Coulée Verte and Bois de Vincennes Previsouly printed in the Piedmont Post on February 24, 2021. The winter months are dwindling, but Paris restaurants, cafés, museums, theatres, department stores, and every imaginable entertainment remains closed. Worse, Paris may be experiencing a third wave of Covid-19 with the spreading United Kingdom mutant dubbed the UK-variant. France continues to enforce curfews and ban international travel with no end in sight, though England is predicting some normalcy by mid-May. For now, Paris parks are open, and as the days gently warm, there are greenbelt options to get some fresh air while practicing social distancing. Paris, though not ranked in the world as a green city, has more than 400 parks. Many agree the most admired are Luxembourg Gardens, Tuileries Garden at the Louvre, and Bois de Boulogne in the 16th arrondissement. Buttes-Chaumont at Belleville in the 19th district is an enchanting city park in the Luxembourg style but with a more intimate aura as a country place. Plus, it’s generally not as crowded with tourists. Jardin des Serres d’Auteil is a secret garden of greenhouse exotics at the southern tip of Bois de Boulogne. The Jardin des Plantes, the city’s vast botanical garden whose roots took hold for apothecary herbs to treat the Renaissance royals, is a top choice. On its grounds are the National Natural History Museum and academies for botany, mineralogy, and geology, while the gardens and natural history museum are a magnet for energetic children on school tours. La Coulée Verte, from the Bastille to Bois de Vincennes A high line park was built atop an obsolete railway spur from the Place de la Bastille to Bois de Path along Coulée Verte where an obsolete train track used to be. Aligre market between Bastille and Nation plazas is a good place to pick up fresh produce, meat, fish, deli, and charcuterie before trail walking or afterwards to carry home for dinner. Vincennes, and since its opening in 1993 is a popular greenway. If the idea of converting an elevated train line into a parkway seems familiar, the New York City High Line was inspired by the Paris trail and opened in 2007, running from the meatpacking district to 34th Street. The stairway entrance to this Paris elevated parkway is at the back of the Opéra Bastille along Rue de Lyon. The park, called the “green river”, is not an exact translation of La Coulée Verte. And earlier moniker was Promenade Plantée (the planted promenade). The walkway is a mile and a half of easy strolling through an assorted green trail of paths laden with roses, plantings, and flower gardens, wild greenery, a short canal. At varying locations, it branches into wider spaces with bench seating. Further along, the pathway narrows over the Jardin de Reuilly and snakes downhill to street level for bicyclists and walkers who will arrive at the entry to Bois de Vincennes in another mile and a half. Trail walkers may wish to bring food and drinks on sunny days and choose a scenic spot to picnic at Reuilly park. A favorite Bastille location, Marché d’Aligre with open stalls and covered counters stacked with produce and fresh foods, is open six days a week. A lot of the trail fun is the sheer elevation – walking on a raised platform places you eye to eye with the third or fourth level of buildings. One is peering over the railings at street intersections and gazing at apartments with The Opéra Bastille that opened to grand fanfare in 1989 was built on the spot that Gare de la Bastille occupied from 1859 to 1969. This second opera house designed for the Paris general populace is immense in size, holding: 2,745 seats; a 500-seat amphitheatre; a 230-seat studio theatre; set and costumes workshops; rehearsal rooms; and offices. Controversy has dogged the project including criticism about “disappointing” acoustics. glimpses of balconies and people walking below: it’s an urban adventure. Once you reach Reuilly, it’s decision-time with a half dozen options. From here you can take the stairs to street level to the Viaduc des Artes and stroll by workshops, cottage businesses, cafés, and retailers along Avenue Daumesnil, where the walk returns strollers to the Bastille. More options open when you decide to walk the entire Coulée Verte and reach the Bois de Vincennes. One may alternately catch the 46 bus on Avenue Daumesnil headed south and ride the mile and a half to the park. Vincennes is the largest park in Paris with crisscrossing foot trails clocking some 50 miles in length. Bicycle trails are also abundant. At the entry to Vincennes, Palais-Porte Dorée is an intriguing museum full of curiosities from the time of the French Colonial Exhibition in 1931, and a glorious example of the Art Deco age. Inside the park is a zoo that children love. Lac Daumesnil along Avenue Daumesnil is the park’s largest lake and entertains patrons with rentals of rowboats, bicycles, and pony rides around the lake for kids. Parc Floral is the site for international flower shows and filled with beauty when the tulips and daffodils are in bloom. From Parc Floral and across Lac des Minimes is a tropical plant garden. The 19th C. Paris Age of Parks Each of the 20 Paris districts was reconfigured with charming park-squares during the reign Promenade Plantée, or Coulée Verte, view of the elevated train now a park in Paris 12th district and below the street-level shops known as Viaduc des Artes. Viaduc des Artes has workshops and artsy shops under the red brick arches below the Coulée Verte high line. Gare de la Bastille, about 1900. The railroad spur to Bois de Vincennes ended in 1969.

A lot of the trail fun is the sheer elevation – walking on a raised platform places you eye to eye with the third or fourth level of buildings. One is peering over the railings at street intersections and gazing at apartments with The Opéra Bastille that opened to grand fanfare in 1989 was built on the spot that Gare de la Bastille occupied from 1859 to 1969. This second opera house designed for the Paris general populace is immense in size, holding: 2,745 seats; a 500-seat amphitheatre; a 230-seat studio theatre; set and costumes workshops; rehearsal rooms; and offices. Controversy has dogged the project including criticism about “disappointing” acoustics. glimpses of balconies and people walking below: it’s an urban adventure. Once you reach Reuilly, it’s decision-time with a half dozen options. From here you can take the stairs to street level to the Viaduc des Artes and stroll by workshops, cottage businesses, cafés, and retailers along Avenue Daumesnil, where the walk returns strollers to the Bastille. More options open when you decide to walk the entire Coulée Verte and reach the Bois de Vincennes. One may alternately catch the 46 bus on Avenue Daumesnil headed south and ride the mile and a half to the park. Inside the park is a zoo that children love. Lac Daumesnil along Avenue Daumesnil is the park’s largest lake and entertains patrons with rentals of rowboats, bicycles, and pony rides around the lake for kids. articles.text: Anybody ever had a crush on a movie star? I have. Ingrid Bergman in Casablanca. Diane Keaton in Annie Hall. Jessica Lange in Tootsie. And then there’s Shirley MacLaine in The Apartment. I fell for her when the movie came out in 1960, and Piedmont movie fans got to revisit her charming, pixie performance at last week’s meeting of the Second Thursday Flix Fest in the Center for the Arts. Helmed by Billy Wilder, famed director of Double Indemnity, Sunset Boulevard and Some Like It Hot, The Apartment was a big hit in its day, winning several awards for its actors and creators and a Best Director Academy Award for Wilder. Young and at his sly, engaging best, Jack Lemon plays insurance worker C.C. Baxter, who lends his Upper West Side apartment to company bosses for offthe-books affairs with female employees. When his manager, the coolly self-serving Mr. Sheldrake (Fred MacMurray), begins using Baxter’s pad in exchange for promoting him, Baxter’s heart sinks when he discovers that Sheldrake’s mistress is Fran Kubelik (Shirley MacLaine), the elevator girl at work whom Baxter is crazy about. Tension, and comedy with real consequences, arises as our hero has to decide between the girl he loves and punching up his career. The Piedmont audience generally liked the movie, noting how society has changed from the era of the film, with its blatant sexism and racism (one attendee said it was Billy Wilder’s dark satire of the period), compared to our more enlightened time. We still have a long way to go regarding gender and racial equity in the workplace, people noted. They liked the handsome black and white photography and especially enjoyed Jack Lemon’s performance. The next Flix Fest showing is the 1995 Italian classic, Il Postino, on February 8th. Sponsored by the Rec Department, the Film Fest takes place in the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m., with a showtime at 10:30. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration can be done at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Those attending are welcome to bring snacks or lunch. 35 years of experience in architectural design www.kaplanarchitects.com (510) 361-0223

articles.text: Like many of you, I have a lot of demands on my time: Earning a living, raising two kids, staying fit, keeping in touch with friends, reading the news…. the list goes on. So while feeling a bit overwhelmed and indecisive this morning, I did what I always do in such moments – I spent a solid two hours gardening. I trimmed the lawn, weeded crab grass from around my perennials and native grasses, and raked up four wheelbarrows of oak leaves. I dumped the leaves on my front flower bed, around the perennials I’d just liberated. I almost never throw oak leaves away. They make great mulch, and their presence compliments the natural feel of my oak woodlands habitat. – Marcus Tullius Cicero I felt great about triumphing over those winter weeds before they got unruly. And just as important, being out in the sun and getting the blood flowing lifted my mood and cleared my mind. Not a second too soon, either, as I come to today’s news: I am pleased to introduce myself as the new gardening columnist for the Piedmont Post. I know what you’re thinking. If you’re a gardener, like me, then you’ve already read my bio and you’re wondering in the crotchety manner of gardeners: “What makes this guy qualified?” And if you’re not a gardener, then you’re trying to figure out how I could possibly entertain you every week. Let me just say that I have unlimited stories about gardening. Let’s start with this one. When I was in middle school in the early 1990s, my friend Eric Fowler and I founded our own lawn care business. We were 14 and could not legally drive, but that wasn’t a problem: We had go-karts. Eric is the one who figured out how to make it work. He went to Sears and bought a small trailer of the sort meant to be towed by a riding lawnmower. He put his Honda push mower in Meet Josh Harkinson, the Piedmont Post’s new garden columnist. the trailer and attached it to his go-kart. And that’s how we got around town. We called our company Precision Lawn Care. Our precision did not extend to the legalities. Go-karts are not street legal, so we spent a lot of time worrying about the police. Whenever we saw a squad car, we’d pull into a driveway to make it look like we were at someone’s house. Eventually the police chased us down. An officer got out, told us he’d seen what we were doing and thought it was very enterprising. He had been thinking about it, and wouldn’t arrest us – as long as we kept the trailers attached to the go-karts to make ourselves more visible to drivers. I have learned a lot over the past dozen years about gardening natives and edibles on a property of 10,000 square feet of hilly oak forest, riparian creekfront, and sunny meadow. One of the two side-side houses was built as the personal residence of the early 20th-Century architect Frederick Reimers, whose father, Johannes Reimers, was a noted landscape architect. I’ve tried to keep his spirit alive. I’m looking forward to sharing more gardening stories. Before any more of January slips away, I want to remind you to fertilize your citrus trees. I like to use E.B. Stone Organics Citrus & Fruit Tree Food sold at Ace Garden Center in Piedmont. They say the best time is during the rainy season after the fruit has set. Your oranges and lemons might be looking almost ready to eat by now, but as I told my tree-climbing daughter today, don’t pick them early, or all at once. They will taste sweeter and last longer if you keep them on the branch until the moment you eat them. Josh Harkinson spent 12 years as a staff writer for Mother Jones Magazine in San Francisco. He graduated from Duke University in 1999 with a degree in Environmental Science and Policy, and from the UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism in 2002. He lives along a creek near Piedmont Avenue with two kids, four chickens, and a wife who thinks he spends too much time gardening. 12-MONTHS FINANCING 0% INTEREST WE PAY TAX SALE* *on all installed jobs CL#788850

articles.text: There was a good turnout of 19 readers showed up to discuss Station Eleven at a gathering of the First Mondays Reading Group on January 8 in the Community Hall. The book is a novel by Canadian writer Emily St. John Mandel published in 2014. It appeared on best-of-year lists and has sold over 1.5 million copies. Additionally, a ten-part version of it premiered on HBO Max in December 2021. The novel takes place before and after a fictional flu pandemic, the “Georgia Flu,” has devastated the world, killing almost everyone. The story starts during a King Lear performance in Toronto when an aspiring paramedic, Jeevan Chaudhary, watches as the famous actor playing Lear, Arthur Leander, has a heart attack. Jeevan tries unsuccessful to resuscitate him, and he then comforts one of the child actors, eight-year-old Kirsten Raymonde. Jeevan leaves the theater and receives a call from a doctor friend. He warns Jeevan to get out of the city, as a deadly flu is spreading rapidly and will soon become a full-blown pandemic. Many people who gather The Code Breaker by Walter Isaacson will be the February book up for discussion to mourn Arthur die within three weeks. After fruitlessly waiting for weeks in an apartment for something positive to happen, Jeevan starts a wandering journey to find a new life. Twenty years later, Kirsten is part of a nomadic group of actors and musicians known as The Travelling Symphony. They perform Shakespeare plays and classical music throughout the region. Kirsten can remember little of her life before “Year Zero,” but she clings to a set of graphic novels given to her by Arthur before his death. They are titled Station Eleven. Mandel’s story follows the different characters as they try to survive in this post-apocalyptic world with past and present lives intertwined. Some of them make it, others don’t, but Mandel leaves her readers with hope that civilization is emerging again. The readers started their discussion answering a basic question: did you like Station Eleven or not? All but four said they did. The negative respondents made their case first, saying they weren’t interested in the genre. The plot didn’t interest them and character development was lacking. The post-apocalyptic world was depressing. Some found the first part of the book intriguing, but lost interest in the characters’ ongoing attempts to survive in this harsh world, and not always successfully. The story was obviously the basis for a TV series, which it was. The novel was not a page turner for them, but rather work to get through. However, most readers enjoyed the book. They enjoyed Mandel’s writing style and found her messages relevant and important. The motto “survival is not enough” from the Star Trek movie, is repeated in the story. The readers agreed with the importance of the arts, culture, community, and family for a meaningful life that Mandel suggests. It was also agreed that the book’s impact was greater for the readers today than it would have been in 2014 when it was writStation Eleven by Emily St. John Mandel ten. The group could more easily envision a post-apocalyptic world in our current Covid times. The vision of hope at the story’s end was also appreciated. Some readers thought resourceful survivors, and especially young people, would find ways to continue on. What was probably most appreciated about Station Eleven was how thought-provoking the book is, and the questions it poses. What is really important and needed in our lives? How would we react in survival situations? What types of relationships do we and society need? It was also said that the discussion provided a deeper understanding of the book and these issues. For all, it was a worthwhile conversation and reinforced the value of the First Mondays Reading Group. The group had previously selected The Code Breaker by Walter Isaacson for February and Lucky Jim by Kingsley Amis for March. Darby Gragg presented three new candidates for a book selection and I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings by Maya Angelou was picked for April. The next discussion will be on February 5 at 1:30 p.m. at the Community Hall. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate. Registration is required at https:// bit.ly/3R86PP4.

articles.text: The forecast of rain showers didn’t scare off 21 intrepid members of the Walking on Wednesday group from showing up at the Exedra last Wednesday. Umbrellas were deployed and the shower quickly disappeared. On hand were: Denise Frankoff with her K-9 best friend Chester, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Sherry Jacobs, Noemi Alvarado, Ken Hubbert, Meghan Bennett, Jim Kuo, Pat Keller, Sharona Fischrup, Mark Davis, Albert Chen, Mike Henn, Rick Eigenbrode, Bill Ahern, and Dick Carter. During their walk the week before the group had visited the Piedmont High campus and talk about the school’s past students. The group thought it would be fun to revisit Clint Eastwood, who had been mentioned as a PHS student. A past Piedmont Historical Society article by Gail Lombardi had identified a Hillside Avenue address as Clint’s childhood home, and the group thought it would also be fun to make it an initial destination. The walkers headed down Magnolia Avenue and up Bonita Avenue and past the former home of Clint’s father, Clinton Eastwood, Sr. He was a PHS grad and later a business executive. The group went down Park Way to Hillside and stopped in front of the Eastwoods’ home. Clinton Eastwood Jr. was born in 1930 and is now 93 years old. Eastwood was nicknamed “Samson” by hospital nurses because he weighed 11 pounds 6 ounces at birth. He attended Piedmont Middle School, and from January 1945 to 1946 he attended Piedmont High School. He transferred to Oakland Tech and graduated in 1949. The Eastwood biography presents the story of a teenager from a middle class family who had a circle of good friends but felt alienated from the wealthy and homogeneous Piedmont culture of the time. He rebelled against it and the people associated with it. After high school, Eastwood did different jobs, served in the army, and got started in acting. After many unsuccessful auditions, he was given a minor role in Revenge of the Creature in 1955, which was a sequel to the Creature from the Black Lagoon, and the rest is more history. The group continued down Park Way to Dracena Park. They zig zagged through the park’s trails, going up the seldom-walked upper east trail. They walked through the redwoods along the main trial to the upper trial along Park Way. The walkers made their way Monticello to Lorita Avenue. In the front yard of a home at the corner they discovered two trees with unique, gnarly bark trunks. The cork oaks are a primary source of cork for wine bottles and cork flooring. The group made their way up to the top of this cul-de-sac and found a hidden, narrow path that returned them to Monticello. Across the street is Arroyo Avenue and down it the group went. Charlene Louie lives there and reminded them that the Key System 10 Line train ran down it during the first half of the 20th Century. The group went onto Lower Grand Avenue and went up Holly Place to York Avenue and another path that connects to Ricardo Avenue and the foot of Dracena Park. They returned to the Exedra by way of Blair Avenue and San Carlos Avenue to Magnolia. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group can there is no charge. articles.text: The Boothby family’s first foster dog was a seven-pound puppy that had been thrown over the Oakland Animal Services (OAS) fence where a bush broke his fall. “He had a rough start in life,” said Cindy Boothby, who began volunteering at Oakland Animal Services after hearing news reports of overcrowding there. “He was so comfortable at our house,” she said of her first foster, named Flan. “I realized he could get some training and love and how much better it was for him at our house than at the shelter.” The puppy was adopted within two weeks and the Boothby family has gone on to foster another five puppies, each adopted within a month. “We foster one, take a break, and then when we are ready we foster another. It’s been incredibly rewarding,” she said. With the post-Covid return to in-person work, rising inflation, and Oakland’s affordable housing crisis, an increasing number of animals are being surrendered to OAS. The shelter is over-capacity with intake of medium and large-size dogs outpacing adoptions and a continuing influx of puppies. As an open admission shelter, OAS must accept all dogs, whether or not it has open kennel space. As a result there is a deadline by which they must be adopted, rescued, or fostered. “The changes we have made in the last three years, as well as the tremendous community support that we have received, has made it possible to maintain a historically low euthanasia rate for dogs, but our work is growing harder. We need the help of this community to make sure every one of these great dogs finds a new family,” said Ann Dunn, Director of Oakland Animal Services. Dunn is asking the public to save the life of animals by adopting a dog. Those who want to help but cannot adopt are encouraged to foster through a program funded by Friends of Oakland Animal Services. Piedmonter Jessica McDevitt fostered a senior dog when she learned he otherwise would have to be euthanized the next day for lack of space. “Looking at his sweet photos and video on the OAS website, I couldn’t stand the thought of him being put down,” said McDevitt. After being fostered by McDevitt for three weeks, he was adopted by a couple looking for a senior dog. “He’s leading the ideal life now,” said McDevitt. “He went camping the first night he was adopted and plays with his adopters’ other two dogs.” According to Dunn, fostering saves animals’ lives, alleviates shelter overcrowding and stress, and provides a chance for dogs to become reaccustomed to a home environment, increasing their chances of adoption. OAS provides fosters with initial supplies, ongoing medical services, and support. Dunn says those interested in learning more about fostering or ready to pick up a foster puppy or dog matched to the needs of their household can drop by the shelter on Thursdays from 12-7 p.m. to speak with a foster coordinator or select a foster puppy or dog. Puppies can be fostered individually or in pairs. For more information, e-mail: dogfostering@oaklandsanimals. org. Oakland Animal Services Dog Foster Coordinator Vivian Chu (left) with Caitlin, Cindy, and Andrea Boothby and foster puppies of Piedmont.

articles.text: January weather demands a hot beverage in one hand and a good book in the other. The Indie Next List for January can help you find your next engrossing read. Each list has a different theme, and this list consists of only the newest releases with rave reviews. The American Booksellers Association fights to keep independently owned bookstores alive and thriving. At the start of each month ABA publishes a list of 25 inspired recommendations from independent booksellers called the “Indie Next List.” The titles below received praise from independent bookstore owners from across the country. Go to Indiebound.org/indienext-list for archives of recommendations, more information and ways to order that will support the small book store culture. Mercury Books, Fiction “An extraordinary novel! Mercury is the lyrically written, unputdownable story of the Joseph brothers and the women who hold them together. It is also in act one that we bear witness to the abiding grief of her parents and sister and brother, while George Harvey struggles with his demons a mere 50 yards away. Will he kill again? And will his next victim be Susie’s sister? But as the tension builds, the narrative breaks and Susie is running through undulating, surreal fields or along golden beaches. It’s a bit jarring. That isn’t to say that had her point of view been used sparingly that it couldn’t have been effective. There were moments when it was essential to the plot. But the key word is “sparingly.” There are many fine performances in this film beginning with Saoirse Ronan who captures in a hundred different ways the intense, vulnerable, innocent teen-tween girl. Mark Wahlberg and Rachel Weisz, as Susie’s father and mother, are both excellent. As is Susan Sarandon in a cameo role as the boozy, far from domestic grandmother who arrives wanting to help. And then there’s Stanley Tucci who delivers a quiet, nuanced portrayal as the malevolent and disturbing neighbor. Tucci is such a fine actor that to watch him work is reason enough to see The Lovely Bones. He defines character actor. Always in the background, always extraordinary, a chameleon in his ability to change his appearance, his mannerisms, down to his walk and gestures. He is never the leading man, but always astonishingly good in supporting roles. His career stretches back to 1985, and it’s not hyperbole to say that he has done it all, receiving countless nominations for his fine performances to include winning two Golden Globes. Recently, he played Meryl Streep’s husband in Julie and Julia, and was memorable in The Devil Wore Prada as Streep’s assistant. He is so good, so accomplished in his roles that he makes his craft seem effortless, and it is not uncommon to wonder if he was there at all. But of course he was, essential to every frame of The Lovely Bones. So many of Hollywood’s headline performers are famous for playing themselves, over and over. Audiences enjoy watching them fill the screen, their familiarity comfortable and predictable. They define the term movie star. But Tucci defines the term “actor,” for he can disappear into a role so completely that his character is remembered, not Tucci. The Lovely Bones. Directed by Peter Jackson. Starring Saoirse Ronan, Rachel Weisz, Stanley Tucci and Mark Wahlberg. 2 hrs., 16 min. Rated PG-13. Now streaming on VUDU/prime/MAX/ apple tv. articles.text: Each year as the lighting of Piedmont’s Holiday Tree approaches, Piedmont residents are invited to greet their Piedmont friends by way of donations to PBF’s Holiday Greeting Fund. This year, in addition to PBF’s regular Funds, donors were provided the opportunity to support the upcoming reforestation of Dracena Park. PBF is pleased to report that a large group of Piedmont families a extended holiday greeting to their Piedmont friends while responding generously to the funding opportunities offered by PBF. Almost $30,000 was contributed to PBF, including $8,300 for the Dracena Park project and $11,000 for its General Fund and $8,000 donated to the Sports Facilities Endowment. This is PBF’s newest permanent fund and is expected ultimately to become a vital source of money to properly maintain Piedmont’s many sports facilities. Coupled with other gifts, most notably the $250,000 for landscaping at the Piedmont pool, 2023 is PBF’s most successful year ever. articles.text: and is open as an attraction to tour the chapel commissioned by Saint Louis in the 13th C. and the donjon completed in 1380. This donjon is a heavily fortified tower standing 170 feet tall and built within the medieval fortress. The tower’s walls are six-feet thick; surrounded by a moat, along with gunports, impenetrable wooden doors, and iron-bar latches. The donjon was where the Royals took refuge once the castle walls were breached by the enemy as a last chance to survive. The Vincennes military training field was decommissioned shortly after Lucky for the future, when Louis-Napoléon III granted the forests of Boulogne and Vincennes in 1855, the sites were professionally designed in the early Victorian style, a romantic vision that still works for today’s visitors. The two parks are legendary, conceived with artistry The latest 19th C. scientific methods were applied to construct lakes and drainage systems; roads and foot trails; and install flora and tree plantings of species numbering in the thousands. Each park has a hippodrome for horse racing, and VinThe Vincennes woods date Lac Daumesnil, the largest of four lakes at Vincennes, offers rowboat rentals, bike rentals, and pony rides for the kids around the lake. back to Gallo-Roman times when Paris was called Lutetia, and Romans referred to the forest as Vilcena. Of the two parks, Bois de Boulogne is stately and more prestigious: its boundary conjoins the 16th district’s west side, a locale with vast wealth, truly astounding mansions, private academies, and well-located foreign embassies. Many rich and famous Parisians prefer the 16th arrondissement. When Jacqueline Bouvier attended the Sorbonne before her marriage to John F. Kennedy, the 35th U.S. President, Jackie, a gifted equestrienne, lived on Avenue Mozart, a 10-minute walk to the woodsy horse trails. The 12th district that borders Bois de Vincennes has primarily mid-century residential and some high-density apartment buildings for families, career, and working people, located in southeastern Paris. Two-thirds of the 12th arrondissement is Bois de Vincennes, an ancient forest that now is a public park occupying 2,460 acres. In comparison, New York City’s Central Park has 843 acres. Patricia Forsyth and Michael Mathews decamped to Paris in September 2019 and shortly discovered they understand very little spoken language, though now improving with credit to French lessons. A markedly positive contrast to the state was in college and career readiness, where PUSD scored 76.2% compared to 43.9% of students statewide. Among all metrics, Piedmont scored worst in chronic absenteeism — 8.7% students chronically absent, an increase of 2.8% from 2023. “In 2023, a quarter of California students missed 10% or more of the school year — better than 2022, when 30% of students statewide were chronically absent,” explained Griffin. “PUSD had less students absent but we weren’t moving in the right direction compared to 2022, We have to balance out what is the ‘new normal,’” e.g. more strongly encouraging students to stay home if they feel ill, “and what is impacting our students long-term.” Contracts, labor The board approved contracts for “Business Services” (including $139,000 for labor relations legal services from the firm Fagen, Friedman, & Fulfrost, LLP) and “Special Education” (comprising $49,402 for the placement of a special education student in a “non-public school”). The board and Hawn met to discuss updates about contract negotiations with the teachers’ union (Association of Piedmont Teachers, California School Employees Association) during a 5:30 p.m. closed session, but as “no action was taken,” Hawn said she had no details to share during the open meeting. All documents for the meeting can be found at bit.ly/47tEB80.

pages.text: 32 Wednesday, January 17, 2024 AMERICANS IN PARIS Continued from Page 23 and is open as an attraction to tour the chapel commissioned by Saint Louis in the 13th C. and the donjon completed in 1380. This donjon is a heavily fortified tower standing 170 feet tall and built within the medieval fortress. The tower’s walls are six-feet thick; surrounded by a moat, along with gunports, impenetrable wooden doors, and iron-bar latches. The donjon was where the Royals took refuge once the castle walls were breached by the enemy as a last chance to survive. The Vincennes military training field was decommissioned shortly after World War II. Lucky for the future, when Louis-Napoléon III granted the forests of Boulogne and Vincennes in 1855, the sites were professionally designed in the early Victorian style, a romantic vision that still works for today’s visitors. The two parks are legendary, conceived with artistry and imagination. The latest 19th C. scientific methods were applied to construct lakes and drainage systems; roads and foot trails; and install flora and tree plantings of species numbering in the thousands. Each park has a hippodrome for horse racing, and Vincennes has a zoo. The Vincennes woods date Lac Daumesnil, the largest of four lakes at Vincennes, offers rowboat rentals, bike rentals, and pony rides for the kids around the lake. back to Gallo-Roman times when Paris was called Lutetia, and Romans referred to the forest as Vilcena. Of the two parks, Bois de Boulogne is stately and more prestigious: its boundary conjoins the 16th district’s west side, a locale with vast wealth, truly astounding mansions, private academies, and well-located foreign embassies. Many rich and famous Parisians prefer the 16th arrondissement. When Jacqueline Bouvier attended the Sorbonne before her marriage to John F. Kennedy, the 35th U.S. President, Jackie, a gifted equestrienne, lived on Avenue Mozart, a 10-minute walk to the woodsy horse trails. The 12th district that borders Bois de Vincennes has primarily mid-century residential and some high-density apartment buildings for families, career, and working people, located in southeastern Paris. Two-thirds of the 12th arrondissement is Bois de Vincennes, an ancient forest that now is a public park occupying 2,460 acres. In comparison, New York City’s Central Park has 843 acres. Patricia Forsyth and Michael Mathews decamped to Paris in September 2019 and shortly discovered they understand very little spoken language, though now improving with credit to French lessons. Hawn said this working draft will come before the board for a second reading at their January 24 meeting. Stephanie Griffin, the district’s Director of Instructional Technology, then presented the board with Piedmont results for the California School Dashboard, a survey evaluating the performance of districts statewide “to decide which need additional oversight.” “The headline here is Piedmont is not one of those. In the dashboard’s seventh year, we passed with good colors,” said Griffin. On a scale of 1 (very low) to 5 (very high), PUSD scored highest on its English Language Arts and Math performance (each 5; respectively 3 and 2 statewide). The district’s graduation rate declined from last year by 1.9%. The “non-graduating” numbers include students who have taken alternate routes, e.g. taking additional years to graduate, taking adult ed diplomas, and taking GED or high school equivalency exams, noted Griffin. “We’ve also had more students moving in and out of the district, to private and other schools since the pandemic.” Similarly, the district’s rate of students suspended for at least one day increased by 0.6%, slightly more than the statewide increase of 0.4%, but was lower overall (0.7% total of PUSD students suspended, compared to 3.5% of students statewide). A markedly positive contrast to the state was in college and career readiness, where PUSD scored 76.2% compared to 43.9% of students statewide. Among all metrics, Piedmont scored worst in chronic absenteeism — 8.7% students chronically absent, an increase of 2.8% from 2023. “In 2023, a quarter of California students missed 10% or more of the school year — better than 2022, when 30% of students statewide were chronically absent,” explained Griffin. “PUSD had less students absent but we weren’t moving in the right direction compared to 2022, We have to balance out what is the ‘new normal,’” e.g. more strongly encouraging students to stay home if they feel ill, “and what is impacting our students long-term.” Contracts, labor The board approved contracts for “Business Services” (including $139,000 for labor relations legal services from the firm Fagen, Friedman, & Fulfrost, LLP) and “Special Education” (comprising $49,402 for the placement of a special education student in a “non-public school”). The board and Hawn met to discuss updates about contract negotiations with the teachers’ union (Association of Piedmont Teachers, California School Employees Association) during a 5:30 p.m. closed session, but as “no action was taken,” Hawn said she had no details to share during the open meeting. In the 32nd minute, Piedmont struck when Beihn played a long pass to Liu when Alameda’s keeper rushed out of net to jump on the ball. However, she didn’t control the ball allowing Liu to recover and send a centering pass to Wallway, who slotted the ball into the empty net with the goa keeper out of position. Liu had a chance to score in a 1-on-1 situation in the 40th, but couldn’t chip the ball over Alameda’s keeper. The Hornets scored an inadvertent goal firsthalf stoppage time when a cross attempt landed in the net. Alameda scored 12 minutes into the second half when a ball settled atop the penalty area, leading to Reese Grifith landed a line-drive shot into net. One minute later, Piedmont’s Ryo Woltag hit the crossbar with a lob attempt over the keeper, while Liu had a near chance go over the net in the 69th. In the 70th minute Piedmont scored on a counter-attack after Alameda was stuffed near midfield, leading to a ball redirected into the path of Wallway. In a 1-on-1 situation, Wallway slotted home her shot to the right of the keeper. Elsa had another shot attempt go wide in the 73rd and Liu had a shot on target three minutes later.
